name: Command-Query Separation
intent: Let a method either answer a question or change something, not both, so that reading is always safe to repeat, reorder or add; and know the few places where doing both in one step is the correct design.
scenario: A cart has a subtotal of 100 and a one-time coupon of 10, so its total should read 90 every time. In the first design total() also spends the coupon the first time it is called; in the second, applyCoupon() is a command and total() only reads. Then a ticket counter starting at 7 is shared by two workers: one design hands out tickets with a single atomic call, one splits it into peek() and advance(), and a third keeps the query pure but names one atomic exception.
problem: A method that looks like a read but also changes state makes the code hard to reason about. Calling it twice gives different answers, adding a log line or a debugger watch changes the result, and the order in which callers happen to read decides what each one sees. Moving the change into its own, visibly named command fixes that. The opposite mistake is to apply the rule so strictly that an operation which must be indivisible, like taking the next ticket, is split into a peek and an advance. Two callers can then both peek the same value before either advances, and both get the same ticket.

howItWorks.title: Sort every method into a question or an order
howItWorks.text: A query returns a value and leaves the observable state of the object as it found it. A command changes state and returns nothing useful (or only an acknowledgement or error). Bertrand Meyer's wording is that asking a question should not change the answer. The test is practical: could a caller call it twice, or call it zero times, and the rest of the program not care?

howItWorks.title: Spot the surprising read
howItWorks.text: In the cart, total() spends the coupon on its first call. The page that reads it three times shows 90, 100, 100. A developer who adds one debug log line that reads the total first makes the whole page show 100, because the log line spent the coupon. Nothing in the name total() warned anyone. Lazy caching is not a violation if nobody can observe it; a read that changes what the next read returns is.

howItWorks.title: Pull the change out into a named command
howItWorks.text: applyCoupon() is called once at checkout, on purpose, and total() becomes a pure calculation: 90, 90, 90, however often it is called, in whatever order, by whichever caller. Pure queries can be cached, logged, asserted on in a test, evaluated in a debugger and called from several threads without coordination. The command is now the only place to look when the state is not what you expected.

howItWorks.title: Know the deliberate exceptions
howItWorks.text: Some operations must read and change in one indivisible step: pop on a stack, increment-and-get on a counter, compare-and-set, the next ticket or id. Split into a peek and an advance, two workers both peek 7, both advance, and both are issued ticket 7 while the counter jumps to 9 and ticket 8 is lost. The atomic call returns 7 to one worker and 8 to the other. Meyer himself notes that stack pop is the classic case, and atomic operations in concurrent code exist for exactly this reason.

howItWorks.title: Keep the exception small, named and documented
howItWorks.text: The healthy pattern is to keep every other method a clean query or a clean command and give the indivisible ones an honest name (takeTicket, popAndReturn, incrementAndGet) and a comment saying why. The same shape applies beyond objects: in CQRS the read model is separate from the write model, and an HTTP GET should be safe to repeat. At each scale the idea is that the reader of the code, and the machine retrying a request, can tell which calls are safe.

pros: Queries are safe to repeat, reorder, cache, log and call from a debugger or a test, because they change nothing
A wrong state has a short list of suspects: only the commands can have caused it
Tests are simpler: a query is checked by calling it, a command by calling it and then asking
Scales up cleanly: safe GET requests, read replicas and CQRS read models are the same rule at a bigger size
cons: Two calls where one used to do, and callers must remember to call the command before the query
Operations that must be indivisible cannot be split without introducing a race, so the rule has exceptions
Some real cases (lazy loading, caches, statistics counters) change internal state on a read; deciding what counts as observable takes judgement
Fluent builders and chained calls return the object on purpose, which looks like a violation but is a style choice, not a surprise
whenToUse: Domain objects and services with state, where a repeated or reordered read must not change what happens next
APIs where retries, prefetching, crawlers or caches may call a read any number of times (a GET should be safe)
Code that is hard to test or debug because looking at it changes it
Any code with concurrency: it keeps the reads lock-free and the writes few and visible
whenNotToUse: To split an operation that must be atomic, such as taking the next id, popping a queue, compare-and-set or decrementing stock only if there is enough
To remove every internal side effect: a cache fill, a lazy load or a hit counter that no caller can observe is fine
As a reason to make commands return nothing at all: returning a result or an error from a command is normal and useful
In throwaway scripts and pure data-processing code, where there is no shared state to surprise anyone
pitfalls: A getter that does work: getTotal() recalculates, spends a coupon, marks an item as read or opens a connection, so the first call and the second call differ
Adding a log line or watch expression that calls a mixed method and changing the behaviour of the program that you are trying to inspect
Splitting an atomic operation to follow the rule: peek() then advance() gives two workers the same ticket and loses a number; the fix is one named atomic call, not a lock around the two
Treating the rule as a ban on commands that return something: a command that returns the new id or an error is fine, a query that quietly changes state is the problem
Calling lazy initialisation and caching violations: if no caller can tell, the observable state is unchanged, and rewriting them as commands adds noise
Using exceptions as a licence: once pop, next and take are allowed to mix, every method starts to mix; keep the exceptions few, named and commented
Forgetting that a GET handler with a side effect is the same bug at a larger scale: a prefetching browser, a crawler or a retry will trigger it

roles.label: Caller
roles.description: Code that asks questions and gives orders, and wants to know which is which.

roles.label: Query
roles.description: Returns a value and changes nothing observable.

roles.label: Command
roles.description: Changes state on purpose and is the only place to look for who did it.

roles.label: Mixed method
roles.description: Reads and changes in one call: a trap when accidental, correct when it must be atomic.

roles.label: Shared state
roles.description: The coupon or counter that the calls act on.

quiz.question: A page calls cart.total() in three places and shows 90, then 100, then 100. total() is the only method involved. What is the most likely cause?
options: The page rounds each value differently, so the same total prints three ways.
total() also changes the cart, for example by spending a one-time coupon.
The cart is cached too aggressively, so it serves an old total.
The three calls ran on different threads, so they raced each other.
quiz.explanation: A pure query returns the same value every time it is called. A first answer of 90 followed by 100 means the first call consumed something. Splitting that into applyCoupon() and a pure total() makes all three reads agree.

quiz.question: Two workers take tickets from a counter at 7. The code calls peek() and then advance(). Both workers get ticket 7. What is the right fix?
options: Add a comment asking callers to call advance quickly after peek.
Make peek() also advance the counter whenever it is called twice.
Have each worker read the counter twice to be certain of the value.
Replace the pair with one named atomic call such as takeTicket().
quiz.explanation: Taking a ticket must be one indivisible step. A single atomic call hands out 7 and 8; two separate calls leave a gap in which both workers see 7. This is the deliberate exception to the rule, kept small and named.

quiz.question: Which of these breaks command-query separation in a way that matters to callers?
options: A getter that sorts a list in place before returning its first item.
A method that caches its result in a private field no caller can see.
A command that returns the new record id after creating the record.
A stack pop that removes and returns the top item in one step.
quiz.explanation: Sorting in place changes what every other holder of that list sees, so a read changes observable state. A hidden cache is not observable, returning an id from a command is harmless, and pop is the documented deliberate exception.
